title: Texas property tax, 11 days of posts

clusters.text: US homes are the least affordable on record, requiring more income than the typical household earns.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The second half of the claim holds up. Redfin's 2026 analysis puts the income needed for the typical US home at about $109,800, 
$22,197 higher than the typical US household income of $87,599
. The Atlanta Fed's Home Ownership Affordability Monitor (HOAM) also shows that a median-income household can't afford the median home. The "least affordable on record" part is contested. The wording matches an Unusual Whales summary of Atlanta Fed data, but that is a secondary aggregator. Redfin says the income needed is 
down 0.5% from an all-time high of $110,382 a year ago
, and that 
the income needed to afford a home has been declining since October 2025
. The Atlanta Fed's own post says July affordability fell to 
the lowest level since June 2025
, which implies it was worse a little over a year earlier. That post does say the median price and monthly ownership cost are 
the highest on record
. Fed Gov. Barr called the July HOAM reading of 68 
the lowest in 21 years
, which is a long-run low but not clearly a record. So "record" is a defensible reading of some price and cost series. As a flat statement about affordability, it conflicts with Redfin's record-high-income-needed date and wi

clusters.text: Home sales are at a 31-year low and mortgage rates hit 7.24% in mid-September.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The 7.24% figure has a real source, but I found nothing supporting "31-year low" for home sales. 
Fortune reported the daily 30-year fixed mortgage rate rose to 7.24% in the week before its Sept. 22 article.
 Mortgage News Daily's index also 
shows 7.24% on 9/16/2026
. The benchmark most often cited as "the mortgage rate" says otherwise. 
Freddie Mac's weekly average was 6.95% as of September 17, up from 6.76% the week before.
 It 
did not reach 7.03% until September 24.
 So 7.24% is a daily lender-quote index reading, not the Freddie Mac average.

On sales, 
NAR reported existing-home sales fell 2% in August to a 3.98 million annual rate, the lowest since June 2025.
 That is a roughly 14-month low, not a 31-year low. NAR's Yun also noted that 
sales over the first eight months of 2026 were up 1.6% from the same period in 2025.
 The "lowest in about 30 years" framing comes from annual totals: 
2024 was the weakest year since 1995
, and 
2025 annual sales remained at a 30-year low.
 I found no NAR or other reporting calling any 2026 reading a 31-year low. The claim therefore appears to stretch earlier annual lows into a current one. The rate figure is defensible only as a daily inde

clusters.text: Texas under Greg Abbott has higher taxes and more data centers.
clusters.verdict_basis:
- Taxes: Total Texas property tax levies did rise, from $73.5 billion in 2021 to $89.4 billion in 2025, 
a 22 percent jump
 according to the Texas Public Policy Research dashboard. That dashboard uses Comptroller data. Abbott's own site concedes that 
many Texans did not feel his reforms because local jurisdictions raised their taxes even more
. But one analysis of Comptroller figures found the levy per $100 of market value 
fell from about $1.95 in 2014 to about $1.58 in 2025
. Compared with other states, the Tax Foundation ranks Texas 
#6 lowest at 8.6%
 for total state-and-local burden. WalletHub puts its property tax burden 
9th highest
 but its overall burden 36th. "Higher taxes" is therefore true for dollar levies over time and for property taxes, but not for the overall burden or for rates.
- Data centers: Counts depend on the tracker. Pew, using Data Center Map figures, counted 
398 operating data centers in Virginia and 296 in Texas
 in early 2026. Other trackers put Texas first on total listings or pipeline, for example 
898 tracked projects
 at PoweredByWho. Texas has clearly added many, but "more" is true only against its own past or against most states. It is not true

clusters.text: Greg Abbott wants to eliminate school property taxes for Texas homeowners.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The claim matches Abbott's stated position. At a Pasadena campaign event he said the local school district portion of a homeowner's bill "should be zero dollars" (
Click2Houston, Oct. 7, 2026
). His five-point plan's last item is 
a constitutional amendment asking voters whether to eliminate school district property taxes for homeowners
 (KWTX). His press secretary told CBS News Texas that Abbott wants policy that 
"eliminates the school district property tax for homeowners"
. Two details qualify the claim without making it inaccurate. The elimination applies to homesteads, so it covers homeowners and not renters or businesses. It would also need voter approval of a constitutional amendment, and 
Abbott estimated state funding would replace the lost revenue at about $10 billion
. I did not check the $3,000 savings figure or the local-budget details, because the claim as worded doesn't depend on them.

clusters.text: Ken Paxton as Attorney General blocked cities from raising property taxes.
clusters.verdict_basis:
The Texas Tribune reported on May 14, 2026 that 
Paxton's office told more than 130 Texas cities they can't raise property taxes because they're not complying with a new state law
. The Houston Chronicle reported a separate batch, saying 
116 more cities will be prohibited from raising their property tax rates after failing to meet a new state auditing law
. Paxton's office announced a further batch of 110+ cities in August 2026 (Texas Scorecard, Townhall quoting the AG's release). The wording matches the Tribune's own headline, so "blocked cities" is accurate as stated. Two qualifiers matter. The ban comes from SB 1851, a 2025 law, which 
bars cities from raising more in property taxes than the previous year if they don't conduct an annual audit and release a financial statement
. And the targets are non-compliant cities, mostly small ones, not cities in general. Paxton enforced that law by sending letters. The claim would be wrong if read as a blanket block on all city tax increases, or as something Paxton did on his own authority. It is not wrong as worded.
